Pakistan's Diversified Industrials Sector Faces Severe Financial Strain as Credit Tightens

Pakistan’s Diversified Industrials sector is facing mounting financial turmoil, as a deepening credit freeze has left firms struggling to meet obligations and continue operations. The crisis, which began to intensify earlier this month, has seen banks and financiers sharply curtail lending to the sector, citing rising default risks and deteriorating balance sheets.

Industry executives are warning that the crunch is threatening the viability of many businesses. "Access to working capital has nearly evaporated in the last three weeks," said Naveed Khattak, Chief Financial Officer at Multan Integrated Industries. "We are unable to secure short-term loans to purchase raw materials or cover payroll. The uncertainty is unprecedented."

Several factories across Punjab and Sindh have reported temporary shutdowns or significant scaling back of shifts. At least six plants operated by leading diversified groups have reduced output, with thousands of workers now on partial furlough or facing delayed wage payments. According to the Pakistan Diversified Industrials Association (PDIA), more than 18,000 jobs are currently at risk if the credit freeze persists through the next quarter.

"The sector is experiencing acute stress, especially among mid-sized enterprises," stated PDIA spokesperson Farah Aslam. "In some cases, projects are stalled halfway, and companies are struggling to maintain even essential maintenance at their production sites."

The credit squeeze has also led to a sharp spike in borrowing costs. PDIA data indicate average interest rates on short-term credit lines have surged by over 400 basis points in the past month. Several firms have reported missing scheduled repayments, triggering further restrictions from lenders.

Site managers at industrial zones in Karachi and Faisalabad report rising absenteeism as uncertainty grows about future employment. "Morale among our workforce is the lowest I have seen," said Saeed Raza, site director at Capital Allied Works. "We are doing everything we can to keep the plant running, but we are dependent on external financing."

Analysts warn that, unless liquidity is restored, the crisis could deepen further, with more shutdowns and layoffs likely. The situation remains highly fluid as talks continue between industry leaders and financial institutions.
